data.content_ref: inline:The target's defense is internally inconsistent because its stated mechanism ('maximizing falsifiability potential,' 'keeping the error-elimination process most active') does not support its actual prescription (preferring the most-corroborated theory). In Popper's framework, falsifiability is an a priori logical property of a theory's content; it does not increase when a theory survives tests. A well-corroborated theory has already had much of its falsifiability potential actualized—its risky predictions have been checked and survived—so choosing it for action leaves FEWER remaining opportunities for error-elimination than choosing an equally content-rich but less-tested theory. The mechanism's own logic ('keeping error-elimination most active') would therefore favor the most falsifiable UNTESTED theory, the opposite of the prescription. Because the operative criterion is actually corroboration (past survival of severe tests) mislabeled as 'falsifiability potential,' the preference covertly relies on past performance to guide future action—the very inductive inference the target claims to avoid. The re-framing fails to escape induction; it merely renames it.
